definition: Just beginning and not yet fully formed or organized.
example: An inchoate sense of unease gradually became a specific concern.
nuance: Inchoate emphasizes lack of formation, not merely novelty.
options: Her inchoate proposal contained a promising instinct but no clear plan yet.
Her inchoate proposal was complete and fully polished.
Inchoate meant that the project was finished years ago.
The proposal was inchoate because its final design was precise.
reasons: An emerging but unformed proposal is inchoate.
A fully formed proposal is no longer inchoate.
A precise final design is developed rather than unformed.

practice.prompt: A music student has just started writing her first composition for the school orchestra.
options: The violin sounded inchoate because one of its strings had slipped badly out of tune.
The inchoate folk song had been sung in the village for three hundred years.
The tune was still inchoate, just a few hummed phrases with no chorus or ending.
By opening night, the inchoate symphony had been rehearsed note for note by the full orchestra.
reasons: A string out of tune is a pitch problem and has nothing to do with an early stage of growth.
A song passed down for centuries is long settled, the opposite of something just starting.
Scattered phrases with no structure yet are an early, unshaped stage of the piece.
A finished piece rehearsed in every detail is fully developed, not still forming.
